<|channel|>analysis<|message|>We need to determine from the paper: Whenever can Chinese courts directly apply treaties? The options: A. Incorporating treaty obligations into domestic law through national legislation or law amendments. B. When stipulated within the Chinese legal system that treaties can be applied. C. Giving precedence to international treaties in accordance with the treaty provisions. D. Applying international treaties based on the contractual agreement of the parties.

Which is correct? We read the paper: The paper indicates that Chinese courts can directly apply treaties in cases with foreign elements, particularly in civil and commercial areas, often when the treaty has a corresponding domestic law (transformation) or is explicitly incorporated; also when the court's normal procedural rule is that if treaty differs, treaty applies, unless it has reservations (Article 189 of Civil Procedure Law). Also, courts can apply treaty provisions in decisions, especially when the treaty is in force; but the direct application depends on statutory provisions: e.g., "if a treaty is incorporated in law or law is amended, etc., or the treaty is explicitly mentioned. B says "when stipulated within the Chinese legal system that treaties can be applied." That seems quite like the scenario: in civil and commercial cases with foreign elements, the rules say that treaty provisions apply if the treaty is applicable. So the question: "Only Based on this paper, please indicate under what circumstances international treaties can be directly applied by Chinese courts:" Could be multiple? But we need to choose one? The question could be multiple choice and choose the letter that best matches the conditions. Look at the text: "On the other hand, in civil and commercial areas, international treaties apply primarily to cases with foreign elements." So there is a direct application via the domestic law's clause that treaties have external applicability as long as there's no domestic conflict. They are not automatically incorporated, but if law says it shall apply, then it can be used. Thus, option B: "When stipulated within the Chinese legal system that treaties can be applied." Option C: "Giving precedence to international treaties in accordance with the treaty provisions." That might be due to the conflict rule in civil procedure (Article 189) that treaty applies if it diverges, etc.

Option A: "Incorporating treaty obligations into domestic law through national legislation or law amendments." This is an indirect method: transforming treaty into domestic law so that the courts apply. But the question says "directly applied" presumably refers to direct application, e.g., if treaty is in force and present in domestic law, the court can apply it directly, as per specific legislation, not by transformation. The paper states the Chinese courts can directly apply treaty provisions under certain legal provisions, e.g., in the civil case: see the case with Shanghai. It said "directly apply the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods" and apply the Vienna Convention. Also, many domestic law provisions, the legal basis for direct application might be Article 142 of the General Principles, Article 238 of the Civil Procedure Law. Those say that the courts can directly apply treaty provisions if they are in force. So the condition is "When stipulated within the Chinese legal system that treaties can be applied."

Thus answer B. But check if any other option matches "When stipulated within the Chinese legal system that treaties can be applied." That is B. I think answer is B. There's no mention that "if parties contract" or "precedence" as four choices one. So answer B.<|end|><|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>\boxed{B}
